name: Recursion, Memoization and Dynamic Programming
intent: Recognise when a recursive solution recomputes the same sub-problems, and fix it by remembering answers (memoization, top-down) or by filling a table in order (tabulation, bottom-up), so exponential work becomes proportional to the number of distinct states.
scenario: A function computes the Fibonacci number for n = 6 by the textbook definition. It makes 25 calls to produce 7 distinct values, and the same fib(4) is worked out twice from scratch. The team then adds a cache, then replaces the recursion with a loop, and finally meets a coin-change problem where the obvious greedy answer is wrong.
problem: Many recursive definitions are short and correct but quietly exponential: each call spawns several calls, and different branches ask for the same smaller question again and again. Fibonacci for n = 40 makes 331,160,281 calls to compute one number that needs only 41 distinct values. The code looks innocent, passes every small test, and then a slightly larger input takes minutes. Separately, recursion costs stack memory proportional to its depth, and some problems tempt people into a greedy shortcut that gives a wrong answer.

howItWorks.title: Count the calls, not just the code
howItWorks.text: Naive recursion makes one call for every path in the tree of sub-calls. If a call spawns two calls and the depth is n, the tree can hold up to 2 to the power n calls. Fibonacci shows it: 177 calls at n = 10, 21,891 at n = 20 and 2,692,537 at n = 30. Big O is about growth, and this growth is exponential: every extra step of n multiplies the work by a constant factor, about 1.6 for Fibonacci.

howItWorks.title: Check for the two signs of dynamic programming
howItWorks.text: A problem fits dynamic programming when it has optimal substructure (the answer is built from answers to smaller versions of the same problem) and overlapping subproblems (the same smaller version is needed by many branches). Fibonacci, grid paths and fewest coins have both. Summing a tree has the first but not the second: each node is reached exactly once, so there is nothing to reuse.

howItWorks.title: Memoize: cache by the state of the sub-problem
howItWorks.text: Top-down memoization keeps the recursive code and adds a lookup: before computing, look the state up in a cache; after computing, store it. Each distinct state is now computed once, so the calls fall to roughly the number of states times the work per state (59 calls for Fibonacci at n = 30). The cache key must be exactly the information the answer depends on: the table size is the number of distinct keys, and that is the real complexity.

howItWorks.title: Tabulate: fill the table in dependency order
howItWorks.text: Bottom-up tabulation drops recursion: a loop fills a table from the smallest states up, each cell reading cells already filled. There are no calls to count and no stack growth, but it computes every cell of the table, including ones the answer may not need. It is often the safer choice for deep inputs, and it makes it easy to see the order of work and to keep only the last row or two when only those are needed.

howItWorks.title: Watch the stack and the greedy trap
howItWorks.text: Each nested call keeps a frame on the call stack, so recursion uses O(depth) memory even when a cache saves most calls, and a deep chain can overflow: Python raises RecursionError at 1,000 frames by default, and other runtimes stop at some limit too. And a greedy rule (always take the largest coin) is a one-pass shortcut that is correct only for some inputs: with coins 1, 3 and 4 and amount 6 greedy uses 3 coins, the optimum is 2. When greedy fails, dynamic programming tries every choice and remembers the results.

pros: Turns exponential time into time proportional to the number of distinct states, often with a one-line change
Memoization keeps the clear recursive definition and only adds a cache
Tabulation uses no call stack and makes the order and the memory use explicit
Finds exact optima where a greedy shortcut fails, such as fewest coins for unusual coin values
cons: The cache or table costs memory proportional to the number of states, which can be large
Recursion depth still costs stack space, and a deep input can overflow the stack
It only helps when sub-problems overlap; otherwise it adds overhead and saves nothing
Finding the right state (what the answer really depends on) is the hard part and is easy to get wrong
whenToUse: A recursive definition where the same arguments show up in many branches (counting paths, edit distance, knapsack, fewest coins)
Optimisation problems built from optimal answers to smaller versions of themselves
Counting problems where only the number of ways matters, not listing them all
whenNotToUse: Recursion over data with no overlap, such as summing or walking a tree: a plain traversal is already linear
When the state space is itself huge (a key with many independent fields): the table can be bigger than memory
When a greedy rule is provably correct for the problem: it is simpler and needs no table
When the recursion is very deep and the language has no tail-call elimination: prefer a loop or an explicit stack
pitfalls: Memoizing when sub-problems do not overlap: the cache adds time and memory and saves nothing, as in a tree sum where each node is visited once

Keying the cache on too much state, such as the amount and the number of coins used so far: equal sub-problems get different keys, the table explodes and hits vanish. The number of distinct states is the real complexity

Using a mutable list or object as a cache key or relying on its identity: it can change after being stored, or compare unequal to an equal value; convert it to an immutable key such as a tuple or a number
Assuming greedy is correct: for coins 1, 3 and 4, greedy makes 6 from 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins) when 3 + 3 (2 coins) is better. Greedy needs a proof; dynamic programming does not need one

Ignoring recursion depth: a memoized function still nests n calls deep for n = 5,000, which overflows the default stack limit in Python (1,000 frames) and may in other runtimes; use a bottom-up loop or an explicit stack
Saying a problem is polynomial because the memoized code looks simple: count the distinct states and the work per state, since a cache over a huge key space is exponential in memory
An unbounded global cache that is never cleared between calls: memory grows for the life of the process

roles.label: Recursive function
roles.description: Computes a value by calling itself on smaller inputs.

roles.label: Call stack
roles.description: Holds one frame per nested call, so memory grows with depth.

roles.description: Remembers answers by state so a repeated question is a lookup.

roles.label: Bottom-up table
roles.description: Filled in order by a loop, smallest state first.

quiz.question: Naive Fibonacci makes 2,692,537 calls at n = 30 and 331,160,281 at n = 40. Why does adding 10 to n multiply the work by about 120?
options: Larger Fibonacci numbers take longer to add, and the additions dominate the cost of each call.
The call stack is copied into fresh memory each time the depth passes another power of two.
The same sub-problems are recomputed from scratch in many branches, so calls grow exponentially.
Each call allocates a new cache, and creating the caches costs more than the arithmetic does.
quiz.explanation: Every call spawns two more and different branches ask for the same smaller values, so the call tree grows by a constant factor per step of n (about 1.6 for Fibonacci). Memoization removes the repeats: 59 calls at n = 30. The arithmetic and the stack are not the cause.

quiz.question: A recursive function sums all 65,535 nodes of a binary tree. A teammate adds a cache keyed by node. What does it change?
options: Nothing about the calls, but it adds 65,535 cache entries: no node is reached twice, so nothing is reused.
The calls fall to about 16, one per level of the tree, because the cache remembers each level.
The calls roughly halve, since a parent can reuse the sum already computed for its sibling.
The recursion becomes iterative, so the stack depth drops to 1 and the overflow risk goes away.
quiz.explanation: Memoization helps only when sub-problems overlap. In a tree each node is visited once, so the cache is pure overhead: the same 65,535 calls and 65,535 stored entries. The stack depth is unchanged, because a cache does not remove nested calls.

quiz.question: With coins 1, 3 and 4, a greedy cashier makes 6 as 4 + 1 + 1. Why is that a problem, and what fixes it?
options: Greedy is only wrong for amounts above 100; memoizing the greedy loop fixes the rest.
The best answer is 3 + 3, since the biggest coin is not always part of the best total; try every coin with a memo or table.
Greedy is right here, and fails only when a coin is missing; add a 2-coin to the set.
Greedy works once coins are sorted ascending; the bug is only the sort order of the coins.
quiz.explanation: A locally best choice (the biggest coin) can lead to a worse total: 4 + 1 + 1 uses 3 coins, 3 + 3 uses 2. Dynamic programming tries every coin for each sub-amount and remembers the best, which is always correct. Greedy needs a proof for the coin set, such as 1, 5, 10 and 25.
